title: Count Patterns Found Inside a Word
statement:
You get a list of strings patterns and a string word. Return how many entries of patterns appear somewhere in word as a contiguous piece.

The list may hold the same pattern more than once; each entry is counted on its own.

examples.why: "ab", "abc" and "ca" are pieces of "abca". "ba" never appears in that order.
"x" is listed twice and counts twice. "zy" is reversed, so it does not count.
a, c and e all occur in order, but not next to each other. Only contiguous pieces count.

hints: For one pattern, the question is just: does it occur in word?
Try every start position in word and compare character by character. Stop early on a mismatch.
Most languages already have this check built in (includes / in). If many patterns were asked against one long word, you could precompute all substrings of word in a set or a suffix trie.

explain.intuition:
Each pattern is an independent yes/no question: is it a substring of word? Answer it for every entry and count the yeses. Duplicate entries are separate questions with the same answer, so they both count.

With word and patterns at most 100 characters, the direct check at every start position is plenty fast. The interesting variant is when the same word is queried many times: then precomputing every substring of the word (a set or a suffix trie) turns each query into a single lookup, like an autocomplete index built once and reused.
steps: For each pattern, check whether it occurs in word (built-in search, or compare at every start).
pitfalls: Checking letters in order with gaps (a subsequence) instead of a contiguous piece, which wrongly accepts "ace" in "abcde".
Putting the patterns in a set first, which loses duplicate entries.
Not handling a pattern longer than the word: the start loop must be empty, not read past the end.

complexity.time: O(p · n · m) worst case for p patterns, word length n, pattern length m

solutions.title: Compare at every start
solutions.idea: For each pattern, slide it along the word and compare character by character.

solutions.title: Suffix trie of the word
solutions.idea: Insert every suffix of word into a trie; every substring is then a path from the root, so each pattern is one walk down.

followups: The word is 100 000 characters long and there are 100 000 short patterns. What would you precompute?
Count the total number of occurrences of each pattern, overlaps included.
lcTitle: Number of Strings That Appear as Substrings in Word
